title: Half Its Money Came From Abroad — Carry On Jatta 4 Just Proved Punjabi Cinema Owns the Diaspora
excerpt: Gippy Grewal's franchise favourite has crossed ₹21 crore worldwide in four days, with overseas markets matching India rupee for rupee — and multiplexes in Surrey, Brampton, and Birmingham are sold out through the week
body:
The numbers tell a story that Bollywood's biggest studios should find uncomfortable. Carry On Jatta 4, the fourth instalment of Gippy Grewal's beloved Punjabi comedy franchise, has crossed ₹21 crore worldwide in just four days — and nearly half of that money didn't come from India at all.

Released on June 26 alongside the much larger Welcome To The Jungle, Carry On Jatta 4 was always going to be the underdog. No Akshay Kumar, no 34-star ensemble, no Star Studios marketing machine. What it has instead is something money can't buy: a franchise that the Punjabi diaspora treats like a family reunion.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=fsDBAr42UUg
"Carry On Jatta 4 has fared better than most Punjabi sequels this year" — Pinkvilla

The opening weekend tells a fascinating story. The film grossed ₹9.35 crore at the Indian box office over its first three days — a strong number for a Punjabi release running on roughly 1,500 screens. But the overseas number is where things get wild: ₹10 crore in overseas gross through four days, with Canada, the UK, Australia, and the Middle East driving the bulk. The film is collecting more money abroad than at home.

Sunday occupancy hit 51.6% overall, with evening shows in Ludhiana touching 62% and Jalandhar crossing 54%. In Chandigarh, night shows were packed at 48%. And those are just the Indian numbers — theatre owners across the GTA, Surrey, and Birmingham have reported near-sellouts for Punjabi-language showings all weekend.

Gippy Grewal returns as the chaos-magnet everyone fell in love with three films ago, joined again by Sargun Mehta, Binnu Dhillon, Gurpreet Ghuggi, Jaswinder Bhalla, and Karamjit Anmol — basically the Avengers of Punjabi comedy. Director Smeep Kang, who has helmed the franchise from the beginning, delivers the same recipe of tangled misunderstandings, family farce, and rapid-fire Punjabi dialogue that has made these films unshakeable. It runs a breezy 2 hours 22 minutes and carries a UA13+ certificate.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DaHI30MyoAe/

What makes the Carry On Jatta franchise special — and why it matters beyond the Punjabi industry — is its audience composition. No other Indian-language franchise, outside of perhaps the Gadar series, draws such a disproportionate share of its revenue from overseas. Punjabi cinema's core diaspora audience — concentrated in Canada's Greater Toronto Area and British Columbia, the UK's West Midlands and East London, and pockets across Australia and the UAE — doesn't just watch these films. They buy out entire screens for community viewings. They show up in groups of twenty.

The previous three Carry On Jatta films were all commercially successful, establishing the franchise as one of the most reliable bets in Pollywood. But the sequel market has cooled significantly in 2026: Bambukat 2, Nikka Zaildar 4, and Godday Godday Chaa 2 all underperformed badly. In that context, Carry On Jatta 4's opening is a reminder that not all sequels are created equal — some are traditions.

Made on a reported budget of ₹22 crore, the film is already close to breaking even in four days. If it can sustain weekday collections in the ₹1–1.5 crore range — and if overseas holds remain strong through the Canada Day long weekend on July 1, which historically delivers some of the best Punjabi box office numbers of the year — a worldwide total north of ₹40 crore is within reach. That would make it one of the biggest Punjabi films of 2026, trailing only Rabb Da Radio 3 (₹30 crore) in domestic gross.

For the diaspora audience, there's a simpler truth at work here. In a landscape where every major Hindi release chases pan-India spectacle and ₹500-crore club memberships, a ₹22-crore Punjabi comedy with no pretensions to global domination is quietly filling theatres across three continents. Because for the Punjabi diaspora, Carry On Jatta isn't just a movie. It's the closest thing to going home.

Where to watch: In theatres now across India, the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, and the UAE. Check local Punjabi showings on BookMyShow (India) or your regional distributor abroad.
